name: Malacca Sultanate
info: A Malay Muslim sultanate founded about 1400 by Parameswara of Singapura, whose port became the great entrepôt of the Strait of Malacca and the model of Malay kingship until the Portuguese took it in 1511.

facts.capital: Malacca (Melaka), at the mouth of the Bertam River, the modern Malacca River
facts.founder: Parameswara, the last king of Singapura, known in Malay sources as Iskandar Shah
facts.predecessor: The Kingdom of Singapura, sacked in 1398; before it Srivijaya and the princes of Palembang
facts.successor: Portuguese Malacca (1511–1641); the Sultanates of Johor and Perak founded by the sons of Mahmud Shah

t: Malacca's rise rested on Ming protection: Zheng He called there in 1407, and in exchange for regular tribute the Yongle Emperor shielded Parameswara from the threat of Siamese attack.

Under Mansur Shah (r. 1459–1477) Malacca conquered Pahang, received Indragiri, Jambi, Tungkal and Siantan from Majapahit and vassalised Siak, ruling much of the Malay Peninsula and the east coast of Sumatra.

Malacca became the centre of Islamic learning in the archipelago; Classical Malay became the lingua franca of Maritime Southeast Asia and Jawi script the medium of its religious and intellectual exchange.
dyk: Afonso de Albuquerque said that taking Malacca from the Moors would ruin Cairo and Mecca and leave Venice no spices but what her merchants bought in Portugal; Tomé Pires wrote that "whoever is lord of Malacca shall have his hands on the throat of Venice".
ev: Parameswara, fleeing the sack of Singapura, founds Malacca at a fishing village of the Orang Laut at the mouth of the Bertam River.
The Yongle Emperor sends Yin Qing to Malacca; Zheng He follows in 1407 and takes Parameswara to China, recognising him as its ruler.
Raja Tengah takes the name Muhammad Shah and the title Sultan, Islamises the administration and issues the Maritime Laws of Malacca.
Ayutthaya invades by land and is beaten with the help of Tun Perak, who becomes Bendahara; a Siamese naval attack is repelled at Batu Pahat in 1456.
Mansur Shah conquers Pahang with a fleet of 200 ships and gains Indragiri, Jambi, Tungkal and Siantan from Majapahit; he dies at the peak of Malacca's splendour.
On 1 August Diogo Lopes de Sequeira arrives from Portugal; a plot to kill him fails, but several of his men are taken captive.
On 15 August Afonso de Albuquerque captures Malacca after a failed assault on 25 July; Mahmud Shah flees south.
The Portuguese raze Mahmud Shah's base at Bintan; he dies at Kampar two years later, and his sons found the Sultanates of Perak and Johor.

sections.foundation:
The Strait of Malacca had been dominated by Srivijaya, centred on Palembang, until the Cholas weakened it in the 11th century, and by the end of the 13th by the Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit. According to the Malay Annals, a prince of Palembang, Seri Teri Buana, who claimed descent from Alexander the Great, landed on Temasek in 1299 and was made king of Singapura by the Orang Laut, the sea people once loyal to Srivijaya. Singapura grew rich in the 14th century, alarming Ayutthaya to the north and Majapahit to the south, and after at least two invasions it was sacked by one of them in 1398. Its last king fled to the west coast of the peninsula: Portuguese sources call him Parameswara, a Palembang usurper of Singapura's throne; Malay sources call him Iskandar Shah, fifth king of Singapura and descendant of Seri Teri Buana.

He reached a fishing village of the Orang Laut at the mouth of the Bertam River, spared by the Majapahit fleets that had sacked Singapura, Langkasuka and Pasai and since the 1370s a refuge that already held Buddhists from the north, Hindus from Palembang and Muslims from Pasai. Legend says Parameswara, resting under a Malacca tree, watched a mouse deer outwit his hunting dog and declared "this place is excellent, even the mouse deer is formidable; it is best that we establish a kingdom here". The founding is conventionally dated about 1400, though earlier dates have been proposed.
sections.socioeconomy:
Malacca grew from a settlement into an entrepôt within a century, thanks to its position on the Strait of Malacca and the demand for goods from East and West. Ships from China, the Ryukyu Islands, Java and the Maluku Islands came in on the northeast monsoon from December to January, and ships for the Indian coasts, the Red Sea and East Africa left on the southwest monsoon. Kedah, Jambi and Palembang were rivals, but none matched Malacca's security, praised in Chinese records of the mid-15th century, nor its port: warehouses where merchants stored goods while waiting for the winds, elephants to carry cargo, and four shahbandars who administered the traders by region. The Orang Laut patrolled the seas against pirates and guided ships in; Arabs, Indians and Persians settled, and the population early rose to 2,000.

Malacca produced little of its own: small amounts of tin and gold and dried fish, with even the salt for curing the fish brought from elsewhere, and rice, vegetables, cattle and fish supplied by its trading partners. Its function was collection and redistribution: cloves, nutmeg and mace from the Maluku Islands; cotton textiles from Gujarat, the Coromandel and Malabar coasts and Bengal; porcelain, silk and iron from China; camphor, sandalwood, spices, fish roe and seaweed from the archipelago. Tin ingots cast in the shape of a peck, each just over a pound, served as a currency unique to Malacca, alongside gold and silver coins.
sections.military:
Megat Iskandar Shah (r. 1414–1424) walled the city with four guarded gates and built a fenced fortress at its centre for the treasury and stores. The chief enemy was Ayutthaya, whose ambitions drove the king to China in 1418 to seek protection, and the Yongle Emperor warned the Siamese ruler in October 1419. In 1446 Ayutthaya invaded by land and was beaten with the help of Tun Perak, chief of Klang, whom Sultan Muzaffar Shah made Bendahara; in 1456, under King Trailokanat, the Siamese came by sea, and Tun Perak and Tun Hamzah, met them off Batu Pahat, where the more advanced Malaccan navy drove them off and chased them to Singapura.

Mansur Shah's fleet of two hundred ships under Tun Perak and nineteen hulubalangs crushed Pahang and carried off its ruler Maharaja Dewa Sura and his daughter; Pahang, Kampar and Indragiri later rebelled and were subdued, and Malaccan forces restored Sultan Zainal Abidin of Pasai against the relatives who had toppled him. After the Vietnamese castrated and enslaved its envoys in 1469 Malacca refrained from retaliation and complained to the Ming court instead. The Laksamana, greatest of them Hang Tuah, commanded the navy and policed the strait. Portugal was another kind of enemy: Diogo Lopes de Sequeira's men were seized in 1509, and Afonso de Albuquerque's armada, arriving in April 1511 to sever the Islamic and Venetian spice trade, failed on 25 July and took the city on 15 August 1511.
sections.governance:
At the head of the sultanate stood the Sultan, an absolute monarch whose right to rule rested on legitimate lineage in the Srivijayan tradition, renamed with the coming of Islam as daulat, sovereignty. The legal codes named four chief officials. The Bendahara, like a vizier, advised the Sultan and kept relations with foreign states, the highest office open to a commoner; the fifth Bendahara, Tun Perak, excelled in war and diplomacy. Below him came the Penghulu bendahari, the treasurer; the Temenggung, chief of police and security; and the Laksamana, head of the navy and chief emissary, who enforced the Undang-Undang Laut Melaka. Four Shahbandars served the trading communities of the port by region, and a Mandulika governed conquered territories.

Malacca was governed by written law, the Undang-Undang Melaka, also called the Hukum Kanun Melaka, and the Maritime Laws, shaped by Hindu-Buddhist tradition, Islam and indigenous adat. Raja Tengah, hearing the ulama Saiyid Abdul Aziz, took the name Muhammad Shah and the title Sultan and made customs, protocol, bureaucracy and commerce conform to Islam; Tomé Pires, however, says Megat Iskandar Shah converted at 72, and it is agreed that Islam was firmly established under Muzaffar Shah (r. 1445–1459). Succession could be violent: Abu Syahid Shah (r. 1444–1446), controlled by his mother's cousin Raja Rokan, was killed with him in a court plot that installed Raja Kasim as Muzaffar Shah.
sections.impact:
Malacca heralded the golden age of the Malay sultanates. It was the first Malay Muslim state to become a regional maritime power and the first centralised polity to rule the whole Malay Peninsula, and for that it is called the spiritual birthplace of Malaysia. From its study centres in Upeh, on the north bank of the river, Islam spread to Jambi, Kampar, Bengkalis, Siak, Aru and the Karimun Islands, through the peninsula, to Java and the Philippines; the rulers of Kampar and Indragiri converted through Muzaffar Shah's influence, and two of Java's Wali Sanga, Sunan Bonang and Sunan Kalijaga, are said to have studied in Malacca.

In Malacca Classical Malay became the lingua franca of Maritime Southeast Asia and Jawi script the medium of religious and intellectual exchange; its traditions, laws, dress, cuisine, performing and martial arts and court rituals set the standard of Malay culture and the pattern for later sultanates, a Malayisation that spread through the region. Rulers came to Malacca after their coronation for the Sultan's blessing, and deposed rulers from the Moluccas, Rokan and Terengganu sought his aid. Malacca carried on the struggle of Singapura and Srivijaya against Java: by the mid-15th century Majapahit could no longer control it, and the spread of Islam into the Javanese interior hastened Majapahit's fall in the early 16th century.
sections.decline:
Malacca was at its height about 1500, when Mahmud Shah rejected the overlordship of both Ayutthaya and the declining Majapahit, but dissension between the Sultan and his Bendahara Tun Mutahir weakened the court. When Diogo Lopes de Sequeira arrived on 1 August 1509 with a letter from Manuel I, the Tamil Muslims close to Tun Mutahir and the Gujarati merchants preached holy war against the infidels; a plot to kill de Sequeira and seize his fleet leaked, and he escaped leaving several men captive. In April 1511 Afonso de Albuquerque arrived to sever Malacca's Islamic and Venetian trade, failed on 25 July and took the city on 15 August 1511. The Portuguese built the fortress A Famosa from the stones of Muslim graves and mosques.

Mahmud Shah fled, tried repeatedly to retake the city, was driven to Pahang and then to Bintan, from which his forces raided and blockaded the Portuguese until they razed Bintan in 1526; he died two years later at Kampar in Sumatra. His son Muzaffar Shah was invited to rule the north of the peninsula as Sultan of Perak, and Alauddin Riayat Shah II founded the Sultanate of Johor. Portuguese Malacca never controlled the trade it had seized; short of money and men, it watched Asian traders bypass it for Johor and other ports, and the single policed emporium of the strait gave way to scattered rivals. The fort fell only once, to the Dutch and Johor in January 1641.

summary: The Malacca Sultanate, founded about 1400 by Parameswara of Singapura under Ming protection, made its port the entrepôt of the Strait of Malacca and the centre of Islam and Malay culture in the archipelago, ruling the peninsula and eastern Sumatra under Mansur Shah before falling to Albuquerque's Portuguese on 15 August 1511.
references: Kenneth R. Hall, A History of Early Southeast Asia: Maritime Trade and Societal Development, 100–1500 (Rowman & Littlefield, 2011)
Anthony Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce, 1450–1680, vol. 1 (Yale University Press, 1988)
Tomé Pires, The Suma Oriental of Tomé Pires, trans. Armando Cortesão (Hakluyt Society, 1944)

pointDescs.1400: Parameswara founds Malacca at a fishing village of the Orang Laut at the mouth of the Bertam River.
pointDescs.1411: Parameswara leads a royal party of 540 to the Ming court with Zheng He; Chinese protection against Siam and Chinese, Arab, Indian and Persian traders make the port grow.
pointDescs.1424: Raja Tengah succeeds as Muhammad Shah, Islamises the administration, promulgates the Maritime Laws and appoints four Shahbandars.
pointDescs.1446: Raja Kasim becomes Muzaffar Shah after a court plot; Ayutthaya's land invasion is beaten with the help of Tun Perak, who becomes Bendahara.
pointDescs.1456: The Siamese fleet is driven off at Batu Pahat and chased to Singapura; Malacca begins to extend its power through the region.
pointDescs.1459: Mansur Shah succeeds; his fleet of 200 ships conquers Pahang and Majapahit cedes Indragiri, Jambi, Tungkal and Siantan.
pointDescs.1477: Mansur Shah dies with Malacca at the peak of its splendour, ruler of much of the peninsula and eastern Sumatra.
pointDescs.1488: Mahmud Shah succeeds as a teenager; Tun Perak and then Tun Mutahir govern and the port prospers.
pointDescs.1500: Malacca is at the height of its power, rejecting the overlordship of both Ayutthaya and Majapahit; it is the chief market of Indian cloth, Chinese porcelain and silk and Malay spices.
pointDescs.1506: Malacca conquers Kelantan, its last expansion.
pointDescs.1509: Diogo Lopes de Sequeira arrives from Portugal on 1 August; the plot to kill him fails and several of his men are held captive.
pointDescs.1511: Afonso de Albuquerque takes Malacca on 15 August; Mahmud Shah flees and the Portuguese build A Famosa from the stones of mosques and graves.

notes: The article's references and further reading sections are empty in the saved text; the references given are the primary sources the article itself cites by name (Tomé Pires's Suma Oriental, the Malay Annals, the Ming Shilu).

The early rulers are disputed: the article treats Parameswara and Iskandar Shah as one person and Megat Iskandar Shah (r. 1414–1424) as his son; Raja Tengah / Muhammad Shah's reign is given as 1424–1444 and Muzaffar Shah's as both 1446–1459 and 1445–1459.
Two peaks (1477 and 1500) follow the article: Mansur Shah died 'whilst Malacca was at the peak of its splendour' and 'by about 1500, Malacca was at the height of its power and glory'.
The 30,000 Vietnamese beheaded is Mao Qiling's claim, presented as such; the Hang Li Po marriage is told only in the Malay Annals and was left out.
The date of Mahmud Shah's death (1528) is inferred from 'the Portuguese razed Bintan in 1526... he died two years later'; the event is dated 1526 to be safe.
